item.title: [BBC World] Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByTiffany Wertheimer, Amy Walker and Joe Inwood, World news correspondentPublished28 November 2026, 12:15 GMTUpdated 14 minutes ago
Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.
The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.
Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.
After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".
In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future".
"Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.
The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.
Buenos Aires argued that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.
The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.
The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

item.title: [CBS News World] Argentina's bid to halt oil drilling off Falkland Islands rejected
item.description:
Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling off the nearby U.K.-held Falkland Islands was rejected Saturday by an international tribunal that rules on maritime disputes.
At a special hearing in Hamburg, Germany, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted 18-3 against Argentina's request to halt drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters, around 300 miles east of Argentina's southeastern coast.
The dispute over the planned drilling revived memories of the bitter war the two countries fought 44 years ago over the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and which have been a British overseas territory since 1833.
In a joint statement, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves welcomed the decision and urged Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders, who number around 3,500 people, to "determine their own future" and end its wider economic pressure.
"This outcome is a vindication of the U.K.'s robust legal defence and strategy," they said. "The U.K. has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders."
In its decision on Saturday, the judges ruled there did not appear to be any basis for believing Argentina had jurisdiction, as the tribunal is unable to make decisions based on questions of sovereignty, Agence France-Presse news agency reported.
Buenos Aires had argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.
Argentine President Javier Milei has vowed to penalize companies working on oil production around the islands and argued that the joint U.K.-Israeli operation is a "clear and present danger" to his country's claims over the islands.

item.description:
A charity set up by the family of a British World War II veteran who raised tens of millions by walking laps of his garden during the coronavirus pandemic has applied to be disbanded, two years after the country's charity watchdog found "repeated" financial misconduct.
An application to have the charitable company created in honor of Capt. Tom Moore removed appeared Friday on the register of Companies House, the official U.K. government executive agency that maintains the public register of British companies, including charitable ones.
Moore, who died in 2021 at 100 years old, raised almost 39 million pounds, or $49 million, through his daily walks in his yard, inspiring people across the U.K. who followed his exploits in daily TV updates during the early weeks of the pandemic. All of the money he raised was donated to Britain's National Health Service.
Captain Tom Moore, 99, poses with his walker while walking a lap of his garden on April 16, 2020.
JUSTIN TALLIS/AFP/Getty
"That's a lot of dollars — isn't it?" Moore told CBS News in 2021.
Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020 during an outdoor investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle, in recognition of his huge charity efforts. He also received about 125,000 cards from the public for his 100th birthday and participated in a charity music single that saw him become the oldest British No. 1 artist ever.
Following the success of his fundraising, his family established the Captain Tom Foundation to continue his fundraising efforts. However, the charity was soon embroiled in controversy and Britain's charity regulator concluded in November 2024 that Moore's daughter and son-in-law personally benefited from the charity.

item.title: [BBC World] Afghanistan explosion kills 10 students and injures more than 100, official says
item.description:
Image source, EPAByJacob Phillips and Mahfouz ZubaidePublished28 November 2026, 10:14 GMTUpdated 59 minutes ago
At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told the BBC.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.
An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.
The province's culture and information director Sami ul Haq Bayan said the blast took place in a house near Shagai Middle School in Asadabad as explosives were being prepared for mining and blasting rock, reports AFP.
The Associated Press also cites the official saying up to 15 wounded people remain in hospital, while the rest have been discharged after treatment.
Pictures from inside a damaged classroom show shattered glass and debris surrounding abandoned shoes and school bags.
Image source, Shutterstock
Footage shared on social media showed several wounded children being taken out of cars and carried into the emergency department at a hospital in Asadabad as a large crowd watched on.
Photos from inside the hospital also show children lying next to each other in hospital beds with bandages strapped around their heads.
Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan but safety standards are often poor, leading to accidents.

item.description:
Doctors Without Borders, also known by their French acronym MSF, said Friday night two of its staff who worked as guards were killed in an Israeli strike on a clinic in Gaza. The Israeli military accused the men of being Hamas fighters.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen," the humanitarian organization said in a post on X. "This is a direct hit on MSF," it added.
In the statement, MSF also said its premises are marked with logos and its locations are communicated to the Israeli military.
"We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability," the statement said.
In response, the Israeli Defense Forces named the two men killed as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, and claimed they were terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.
Palestinians attend the funeral ceremony of Ahmed Abu Hasira.
Ali Jadallah/Getty Images
"While also serving as terrorists, the two worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF). This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the IDF said in a statement released on Friday.
The Israeli military also disputed the claim that MSF facilities were targeted in the attack, claiming that no damage was caused to medical infrastructure. It added that it had used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to minimize "the expected harm to civilians."
MSF say the deaths bring the total number of their workers killed in Gaza to 17.

item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17 ByJames Chater and Rushdi Abualouf, Gaza correspondentPublished28 November 2026, 06:52 GMTUpdated 3 hours ago
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."
In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

More than 1,500 members of Mexico’s Zapatista movement will travel from the southern state of Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of the disappeared and join forces to address the issue of the more than 130,000 people missing across the countryByEDUARDO VERDUGO Associated Press and MARÍA VERZA Associated PressNovember 28, 2026, 12:34 AM

SAN CRISTÓBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico -- More than 1,500 members of Mexico's Zapatista movement will begin a “Tour for Life” this Saturday, traveling from the southern state of Chiapas to Mexico City to meet with families of the disappeared and join forces in addressing the issue of the more than 130,000 people missing across the country.
The Zapatista Army of National Liberation, the guerrilla group known as the EZLN that rose up against the Mexican state in 1994, never laid down its arms but for decades has chosen social activism and the self-governance of its territories as a way to continue fighting for Indigenous peoples and human rights.
Members of the movement will depart San Cristóbal de las Casas in Chiapas in 35 buses and in Mexico City they will provide “thousands of ears” to listen to and embrace those searching for their relatives, according to a statement by one of its spokespeople, Subcomandante Moisés.
Some people with missing relatives were in San Cristóbal de las Casas to meet with the Zapatistas before the trip and they described their situations.
Adriana Pérez said she lost track of her brother in San Cristóbal de las Casas six years ago while he was on his way from home to work. Liliana Pérez, who is not related, said she has two missing sons and complained that the Mexican army never helped her search for them, even though the eldest was an active-duty soldier in Chiapas. item.description:

China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidentsByKelly NgPublished27 November 2026
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Image source, Dolkun IsaImage caption,
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blazeByGrace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese , Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette TanPublished25 November 2026
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
